headline: Would You Cross a Bridge Built on Sam Altman's Word?
lede: Closing arguments in Musk v. Altman — the federal lawsuit over OpenAI's transition from nonprofit to for-profit corporation — produced, on May 14, 2026, both the most memorable rhetorical image of the trial and one of its most embarrassing legal performances. Elon Musk's lead trial counsel, Steven Molo, asked the jury to imagine a wooden bridge suspended over a river gorge, its sole assurance of safety being Sam Altman's word: “Would you walk across that bridge? I don't think many people would.” The image traveled; the chaos around it made it land harder.
body:
Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015 as a nonprofit, donating at least $38 million before departing the board in 2018. He filed suit in August 2024, narrowing his case — after dropping fraud allegations — to two surviving claims: **breach of charitable trust**, the argument that his donations created a binding legal obligation for OpenAI to remain nonprofit, open-source, and unmotivated by private gain; and *unjust enrichment*, arising from the corporate conversion that has made insiders including Altman enormously wealthy on paper. OpenAI is now valued at roughly $852 billion. Microsoft (MSFT), OpenAI's largest external investor, is also a defendant. Musk's team seeks up to $150 billion in *disgorgement* — a court-ordered forfeiture of wrongfully obtained profits — plus Altman's removal and a structural unwind of the for-profit conversion.

The bridge metaphor was Molo's rhetorical capstone. He spent the day cataloguing witnesses who called Altman a liar under oath: Musk himself, Ilya Sutskever, Mira Murati, Helen Toner, and Tasha McCauley. “Sam Altman's credibility is directly at issue in this case,” Molo told the jury. “He's the defendants' main witness. If you cannot trust him, if you don't believe him, they cannot win.” Then came the image: a hiker approaching a wooden bridge over a gorge 100 feet above a river. A woman at the entrance says the bridge is safe — built, she tells you, on Sam Altman's version of the truth. Would you cross? The question was designed to produce an instinctive answer to an otherwise labyrinthine legal claim.

What made the moment darkly comic was everything surrounding it. Molo that same day referred to co-defendant Greg Brockman — OpenAI's co-founder and former president — as “Greg Altman,” fusing him with the man he was arguing against. He told the jury Musk was “not asking for any money” — a statement so plainly at odds with the $150 billion disgorgement claim that Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers interrupted to correct the record, offering Molo the choice to retract or formally drop the damages figure. She ordered a corrective instruction to the jury. Observers described the session as an “unbelievable demolition derby.” The bridge metaphor arrived in the middle of this wreckage, perhaps the one image that would travel cleanly.

OpenAI's attorneys were sharper. Sarah Eddy accused Musk of “selective amnesia” for claiming he never read a 2018 term sheet laying out the for-profit plans — incredible, she said, for one of “the most sophisticated businessmen in the history of the world.” Then she delivered what courtroom reporters flagged as the day's most damaging line: “Even the people who work for him, even the mother of his children can't back his story” — a reference to Shivon Zilis, a former OpenAI board member and the mother of four of Musk's children, whose testimony failed to support his account. William Savitt offered the signature dismissal: “Mr. Musk may have the Midas touch in some areas, but not in AI. To succeed in AI, as it turns out, all Mr. Musk can do is come to court.”

The nine-person jury will begin deliberations Monday, May 18. Their verdict on liability is *advisory only* — Judge Gonzalez Rogers retains final authority over all equitable claims and will issue her own ruling. A finding against OpenAI could complicate a long-anticipated IPO and force a reckoning over the nonprofit Foundation's effective control. What happens to the bridge depends on whether the judge, not the jury, finds the planks sound.

concepts.definition: A legal doctrine holding that donations to a charitable organization create binding obligations on how those funds and the organization's mission are used. Musk argues his $38 million in contributions came with implicit strings: that OpenAI remain nonprofit, open-source, and focused on public benefit rather than private gain.

A legal claim asserting that a defendant improperly benefited at the plaintiff's expense without legal justification, and that a court should order restitution. Musk argues that OpenAI's shift to a for-profit structure allowed insiders to collect enormous stock grants funded by what were originally charitable contributions.

A court-ordered equitable remedy requiring a party to surrender profits gained through wrongdoing, rather than pay punitive damages. Musk's team seeks up to $150 billion in disgorgement, intended to be redirected to OpenAI's nonprofit arm rather than paid to Musk personally.

In equity cases — those seeking remedies like injunctions or disgorgement rather than simple money damages — a jury's finding is advisory rather than binding. The judge may accept, reject, or modify it. In Musk v. Altman, Judge Gonzalez Rogers will issue her own ruling regardless of what the jury decides.
